conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’ll be walking with you through a quick check-in about how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a simple, 10-question screen that helps us see how mood, anxiety, and energy levels have been for you over the past seven days. Nothing you share leaves this room, and there are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. We’ll go one question at a time, and we can pause whenever you need. Ready to start?

In the past week, how often have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly... not much. I used to laugh all the time—my husband and I would joke around every night—but lately it feels like I have to force it. Maybe once or twice this week I sort of chuckled at a silly meme, but even then it faded fast. Mostly I just feel... flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I haven’t. I can count on one hand the times I even cracked a smile, and even then it felt kind of fake, like I was doing it because I “should,” not because anything felt truly funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I still go through the motions—like I’ll think “maybe I’ll feel better if I take the baby for a walk,” but when the time comes it just feels like another chore. I did manage to meet a friend for coffee yesterday, and for a few minutes I sort of looked forward to getting out, but the excitement was gone before I even left the house.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot of the time. If the baby spits up more than usual or won’t settle, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” Yesterday I cried because I couldn’t get her to nap, and I kept thinking, “A good mom would know how to fix this.” I know it’s probably not fair, but the guilt just shows up anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s going to choke, or I’ll lie down and can’t stop picturing the crib sheet coming loose and smothering her. Nothing has to trigger it—my mind just spins. I try breathing like the nurse showed me, and sometimes that calms me for a minute, but the worry pops back up before long.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—at least three or four times this week. It hits out of nowhere, like this wave where my chest feels tight and I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even though I can’t name what. Night before last I was rocking the baby in the dark and suddenly felt I couldn’t breathe—my hands shook so badly I had to hand her to my husband. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me rattled the rest of the night.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It’s like the pile of laundry, the dishes, the feedings, the texts I haven’t answered—they all gang up on me. I’ll stand in the kitchen and just stare because I don’t know which thing to tackle first. Sometimes I manage to push through and fold a load or two, but the feeling that I’m drowning comes right back the minute the baby cries again.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut up. I keep replaying everything I might have messed up that day, or imagining accidents that could happen to her. It takes me over an hour to fall asleep most nights, and when I finally do, I jerk awake at every little sound, heart pounding, convinced something’s wrong. I’m lucky if I get four broken hours.
I have felt sad or miserable

Almost every day this week. It’s like there’s a gray cloud parked over me. I’ll be holding the baby and tears just well up for no clear reason. Yesterday I spent half the afternoon on the sofa crying quietly so my older kid wouldn’t see. The sadness isn’t sharp anymore—it’s more like this heavy blanket I can’t push off.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice since last weekend. Once was after the night-feed when I couldn’t get her back to sleep—tears just started rolling and I couldn’t stop. The other time was yesterday morning; my husband asked how I’d slept and I opened my mouth to answer and wound up sobbing instead. I feel like I cry over anything lately.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Maybe once or twice… I’ll be standing at the changing table and this quick, awful picture flashes—like what if I just walked out the door and didn’t come back. Or I’ll think the kids would be better off if I weren’t here. I haven’t made any plans and I don’t want to die; the thoughts just pop in and scare me. I push them away as fast as I can, but they’ve shown up a couple of times this week.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has faded since your baby arrived: laughter feels forced, simple tasks feel like drowning, and a heavy sadness blankets most days. You described frightening panic surges, nightly battles with racing thoughts, and tearful guilt that you're somehow failing your children. You also courageously admitted fleeting thoughts of walking away or wondering if your family would be better off without you. Your words paint a picture of deep emotional pain that is far beyond typical new-parent stress, and it's understandable that you feel overwhelmed.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no laughter, describing smiles as rare and forced, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports minimal anticipation of enjoyment, consistent with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('a lot of the time') tied to routine infant care and intense guilt, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily anxiety about multiple infant scenarios without clear triggers, consistent with 'very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden, intense panic episodes this week with physical symptoms (tight chest, shaking, breathlessness), matching "Yes, quite a lot".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm ('Most days') and difficulty coping, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption with racing thoughts and frequent awakenings, indicating severe difficulty sleeping most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily sadness with frequent tearfulness and inability to feel better, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two distinct crying episodes in the past week triggered by routine stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive thoughts of self-harm or escape "a couple of times this week" that are distressing but without intent or planning, aligning with "Sometimes."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 26/30 exceeds the ≥14 threshold for probable major depression; Item 10 score ≥1 mandates immediate risk assessment. The patient reports core symptoms meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), significant weight/appetite or sleep disturbance (<sym>insomnia</sym>), fatigue, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, diminished ability to think or concentrate, and recurrent thoughts of death. Frequency of <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic spells</sym>, and <sym>self-harm ideation</sym> indicates severity and safety concern. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist for full diagnostic evaluation and safety plan
2. Call 988 or local emergency services if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Inform a trusted adult who can stay with you tonight for support until professional help is in place
4. Begin basic sleep-hygiene measures (dim lights, delegate night feeds when possible, limit screens after 9 p.m.)
5. Temporarily pause non-essential chores; accept help with meals, laundry, and baby care to conserve energy
6. Explore evidence-based treatments: <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or sertraline compatible with breastfeeding per provider guidance
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS in one week to monitor symptom trajectory
8. Access local <med>Postpartum Support International</med> warm-line 1-800-944-4773 for 24/7 peer support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Period (not diagnostic)

Presenting symptoms
- Marked anhedonia (minimal laughter/pleasure, described smiles as “fake”)
- Loss of anticipatory enjoyment; activities feel obligatory
- Daily pervasive sadness, frequent tearfulness
- Significant guilt/self-blame regarding infant care
- Persistent, intrusive anxiety and panic spells (3–4× this week) with physical symptoms
- Overwhelm and impaired coping with routine tasks
- Sleep-onset and maintenance problems linked to rumination and hypervigilance
- Passive self-harm ideation (no plan/intent): fleeting thoughts of leaving or that children “would be better off”

Patterns/risk indicators
- Consistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, anxiety, functional impairment
- Postpartum insomnia directly tied to mood
- Safety concern: presence of self-harm ideation (requires further risk assessment)

Screening significance: findings strongly suggest possible major depressive episode with anxious features in postpartum context; recommend formal diagnostic evaluation, risk assessment, and discussion of support/treatment options.
